title: It always takes longer
topic: the planning fallacy: why we underestimate how long things take
hook: Why does everything take longer than you planned?
promise: We plan for the best case even when we know our past projects ran late (the planning fallacy).

takeaway.text: Plan from how long it took last time, not from how long it should take.

scenes.narration: Why does everything take longer than you planned?
scenes.visualIdea: A calendar with one date circled; the pages start to fly.

scenes.narration: Week one. Lea plans her thesis: one month, maybe five weeks. She has a plan on the wall.
scenes.visualIdea: Lea at her desk in week one, confident, a neat plan on the wall.

scenes.narration: Week six. Week seven. The plan is still on the wall. The thesis is not finished.
scenes.visualIdea: Weeks pass on the wall; the plan gets covered in notes; cups pile up; it is night.
scenes.setting: the same room, weeks later, at night

scenes.narration: Psychologists call this the planning fallacy. We imagine the best case, and forget how our last project went.
scenes.visualIdea: Two timelines: the plan in a straight line, the real one with detours.

scenes.narration: In one well-known study, students guessed about thirty-four days for their thesis. It took them about fifty-six.
scenes.visualIdea: A study's two bars: the students' estimate and the real time.

scenes.narration: So plan from how long it took last time, not from how long it should take.
scenes.visualIdea: Lea pins her old timeline next to the new plan.

claims.text: Buehler, Griffin and Ross (1994): students predicted about 34 days to finish their thesis; the average was about 56 days.
claims.source: Buehler, Griffin & Ross, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1994
